etymology: Of uncertain Northern origin. The plural occurs twice in the KJV, and the two places could hardly be further apart — the twin sons of Isaac growing up in Canaan, and the children Zechariah promises will play in the streets of a restored Jerusalem.
biblical_def: The first use covers twenty years in four words: “And the boys grew: and Esau was a cunning hunter, a man of the field; and Jacob was a plain man, dwelling in tents” (Genesis 25:27). The divergence had been announced before they were born: “And the LORD said unto her, Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger” (Genesis 25:23). The second use is a promise given to a city in ruins, and it is one of the tenderest pictures of restoration in the prophets: “And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in the streets thereof” (Zechariah 8:5). The verse before it sets the other end of the same street: “Thus saith the LORD of hosts; There shall yet old men and old women dwell in the streets of Jerusalem, and every man with his staff in his hand for very age” (Zechariah 8:4). God measures the restoration of a city by the safety of its oldest and its youngest in the open street.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines boy as a male child, from birth to the age of puberty; a lad.
webster_full: BOY, n. A male child, from birth to the age of puberty; but in general, applied to males under ten or twelve years of age.
CHILD, n. A son or a daughter; a male or female descendant, of any degree of distance from the parent.
PLAY, v.i. To sport; to frolic; to frisk; to do something not as a task or for profit, but for amusement.
NURTURE, n. That which nourishes; education; instruction; the discipline and admonition of the Lord.
POSTERITY, n. Descendants; children, children's children, and so on indefinitely.
scriptures: Genesis 25:27
And the boys grew: and Esau was a cunning hunter, a man of the field; and Jacob was a plain man, dwelling in tents.
Genesis 25:23

And the LORD said unto her, Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger.
Zechariah 8:5
And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in the streets thereof.
Zechariah 8:4
Thus saith the LORD of hosts; There shall yet old men and old women dwell in the streets of Jerusalem, and every man with his staff in his hand for very age.
corruption_summary: Children are counted as a cost or a lifestyle choice, against a Bible that calls them a heritage of the LORD and makes their play in the street a picture of a city God has healed.
corruption_paragraphs: Zechariah 8:5 is a quiet rebuke to the way a generation now reasons about children. The prophet is describing a restored Jerusalem, and the two details he selects are old people sitting in the street because they are too old to walk far, and boys and girls playing in it. Both are signs of a city safe enough that its most vulnerable can be outdoors. A society that measures its health by output and treats children principally as an expense has adopted an accounting Scripture nowhere uses: lo, children are an heritage of the LORD, and the fruit of the womb is his reward.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover from Genesis 25 is different and equally needed. The boys grew, and they grew in opposite directions in the same tent, under the same parents, with the divergence announced before their birth and each parent choosing a favourite. Scripture records covenant households whose children went different ways without flinching, and it does not permit either the fatalism that stops praying or the presumption that treats upbringing as a mechanism. Parents are commanded to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. The outcome belongs to the God who spoke to Rebekah before either boy drew breath.

“Full of boys and girls playing in the streets” — the sign of a healed city.
“There shall yet old men and old women dwell in the streets” — the other end of it.

pos: n. pl. (a class of Babylonian provincial officials)
etymology: An English word of Saxon origin — shire-reeve, the king's officer in a county — used by the translators to render an Aramaic term for a class of magistrates. It occurs twice, both in the summons to Nebuchadnezzar's image.
biblical_def: Nebuchadnezzar summons the entire administrative apparatus of an empire to one ceremony: “Then Nebuchadnezzar the king sent to gather together the princes, the governors, and the captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, to come to the dedication of the image which Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up” (Daniel 3:2). The list is then repeated verbatim as they arrive: “Then the princes, the governors, and captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, were gathered together unto the dedication of the image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up; and they stood before the image” (Daniel 3:3). The repetition is deliberate and heavy; seven ranks of officialdom, named twice, standing in a plain. The command is total: “That at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, ye fall down and worship the golden image” (Daniel 3:5). Against the whole weight of it stand three men with one sentence: “But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up” (Daniel 3:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sheriff as an officer in each county to whom is entrusted the execution of the laws; the translators use it for a Chaldean magistrate.
webster_full: SHERIFF, n. An officer in each county, to whom is entrusted the execution of the laws; from shire and reeve.
MAGISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.
PROVINCE, n. A country belonging to a kingdom or state, either by conquest or colonization.
DEDICATION, n. The act of consecrating to a divine Being, or to a sacred use.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge; the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions.
scriptures: Daniel 3:2

Then Nebuchadnezzar the king sent to gather together the princes, the governors, and the captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, to come to the dedication of the image which Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up.
Daniel 3:3

Then the princes, the governors, and captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, were gathered together unto the dedication of the image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up; and they stood before the image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up.
Daniel 3:5

That at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp , sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, ye fall down and worship the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king hath set up:
Daniel 3:18
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
corruption_summary: Conscience is treated as a private preference the state may override for the common good, when Daniel 3 sets the whole machinery of an empire against three men and vindicates the three.
corruption_paragraphs: Daniel 3 is built to make the reader feel the asymmetry. Seven grades of official are listed twice, six instruments are named, the furnace is heated seven times, and the king asks the question every persecutor asks: who is that God that shall deliver you out of my hands? The answer the three give is the high-water mark of creaturely faith in the Old Testament, and its strength lies in the middle clause. They say God is able to deliver them; they say He will deliver them; and then they say but if not, we will not serve thy gods. Their obedience was not contingent on the outcome.

The doctrine is the limit of the civil magistrate. Scripture commands submission to governing authorities as ordained of God, and the same Scripture records Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refusing an imperial decree, the apostles answering the Sanhedrin that we ought to obey God rather than men, and the midwives of Egypt lying to Pharaoh and being blessed for it. The magistrate's sphere is real and God-given; it does not extend to the conscience, and where it commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands it must be disobeyed and the penalty accepted. That is the classical Reformed position, and it is why the sheriffs are in the list: to show the reader exactly how much was standing on the other side.

“They stood before the image” — the same list, arrived.
“But if not…we will not serve thy gods” — three men against all of it.

pos: n. (a son of Esau by Aholibamah, and a duke of Edom)
etymology: Hebrew Yalam, meaning hidden or concealed. He is one of the sons born to Esau in Canaan, and one of the chiefs whose houses became the nation of Edom.
biblical_def: He is named at his birth: “And Aholibamah bare Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah: these are the sons of Esau, which were born unto him in the land of Canaan” (Genesis 36:5). The genealogy is repeated as the chapter organises Esau's house: “And these were the sons of Aholibamah, the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon, Esau's wife: and she bare to Esau Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah” (Genesis 36:14). And the same three are then listed as rulers: “And these are the sons of Aholibamah Esau's wife; duke Jeush, duke Jaalam, duke Korah: these were the dukes that came of Aholibamah the daughter of Anah, Esau's wife” (Genesis 36:18). Genesis 36 is a long chapter, and its point is made plain at the end of the list of Edomite kings: “And these are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel” (Genesis 36:31). Esau's line had dukes and kings and territory generations before Jacob's had anything but a promise.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines duke as a chief or leader; in Scripture, the chiefs of the families descended from Esau in Edom.
webster_full: JAALAM, n. A son of Esau by Aholibamah, and a duke of Edom; in Hebrew, hidden.
DUKE, n. In Scripture, a chief or leader of a family or clan; the heads of the houses of Edom.
EDOM, n. The country of the descendants of Esau, south and southeast of the Dead Sea; also called Idumea.
BIRTHRIGHT, n. Any right or privilege to which a person is entitled by birth; the right of the firstborn.
ELECTION, n. The act of choosing; divine choice; predetermination of God, by which persons are distinguished as objects of mercy.
scriptures: Genesis 36:5
And Aholibamah bare Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah: these are the sons of Esau, which were born unto him in the land of Canaan.
Genesis 36:14
And these were the sons of Aholibamah, the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon, Esau's wife: and she bare to Esau Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah.
Genesis 36:18
And these are the sons of Aholibamah Esau's wife; duke Jeush, duke Jaalam, duke Korah: these were the dukes that came of Aholibamah the daughter of Anah, Esau's wife.
Genesis 36:31
And these are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel.
corruption_summary: Visible prosperity is read as a sign of divine favour, when Genesis deliberately shows Esau's line established with dukes and kings while Jacob's held only a promise.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 36 is skipped by nearly every reader, and its placement is an argument. Jacob has just come home, buried his father, and settled in a land he does not own; the narrative then devotes a full chapter to Esau — his wives, his eleven dukes, his eight kings, and the plain observation that these reigned in Edom before there reigned any king over the children of Israel. The chosen line looks, at this point in the story, like the losing one. Scripture arranges it that way on purpose, and it is the standing corrective to any doctrine that reads present prosperity as a verdict on standing before God.

Paul takes these two brothers as his central case for unconditional election, quoting Malachi's Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated, and grounding the choice explicitly in God's purpose rather than in anything either child had done, since the word came before they were born or had done any good or evil. The dictionary holds that reading without softening it. Esau was not a monster; he was a capable man who founded a nation, forgave his brother, and prospered. The difference between the lines was not merit and was never presented as merit. It was the purpose of God according to election.

pos: n. (a son of Eliphaz and duke of Edom)
etymology: Hebrew Tsepho, meaning watch or lookout; the Chronicler spells it Zephi. He is a grandson of Esau through Eliphaz, and one of the dukes of Edom.
biblical_def: He appears in the roll of Esau's grandsons: “And the sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Gatam, and Kenaz” (Genesis 36:11), and again among the chiefs: “These were dukes of the sons of Esau: the sons of Eliphaz the firstborn son of Esau; duke Teman, duke Omar, duke Zepho, duke Kenaz” (Genesis 36:15). His brother Teman gave his name to the district from which Job's friend Eliphaz the Temanite came, and another line of the same family produced Amalek: “And Timna was concubine to Eliphaz Esau's son; and she bare to Eliphaz Amalek: these were the sons of Adah Esau's wife” (Genesis 36:12). That single verse is the origin of the nation that attacked Israel at Rephidim and against which God swore perpetual war. Centuries later the prophets speak to Edom in terms that assume this kinship: “For thy violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee, and thou shalt be cut off for ever” (Obadiah 1:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Zepho; the Hebrew signifies a watch or lookout, and the name belongs to a grandson of Esau and duke of Edom.
webster_full: ZEPHO, n. A son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau; one of the dukes of Edom.
ELIPHAZ, n. The firstborn son of Esau; also the name of the Temanite, first of Job's three friends.
AMALEK, n. A son of Eliphaz by Timna, and the nation descended from him, inveterate enemies of Israel.
KINDRED, n. Relation by birth; relatives by blood; affinity; a family or race.
ENMITY, n. The quality of being an enemy; ill will; hatred; a state of opposition.
scriptures: Genesis 36:11
And the sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Gatam, and Kenaz.
Genesis 36:15
These were dukes of the sons of Esau: the sons of Eliphaz the firstborn son of Esau; duke Teman, duke Omar, duke Zepho, duke Kenaz,
Genesis 36:12
And Timna was concubine to Eliphaz Esau's son; and she bare to Eliphaz Amalek: these were the sons of Adah Esau's wife.
Obadiah 1:10
For thy violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee, and thou shalt be cut off for ever.
corruption_summary: Family enmity is treated as a merely private matter, when Scripture traces a national hatred back to one household and holds a nation accountable for it centuries later.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture reckons with generational consequence without abandoning individual responsibility. The list of dukes in Genesis 36 includes, almost in passing, the birth of Amalek to a concubine of Eliphaz, and from that verse runs the whole later history: the ambush at Rephidim, the war God swore from generation to generation, Saul's partial obedience, Haman the Agagite's decree. One household's arrangements produced a nation's enmity.

Obadiah shows how the accounting is finally made, and it is worth noticing how it is framed. Edom is not condemned for existing or for descending from Esau; it is condemned for what it did, and the charge is specific — violence against thy brother Jacob, standing on the other side in the day that strangers carried away his forces, rejoicing over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction. The biblical categories are the actual deeds of actual people, with the kinship making the guilt worse rather than supplying it. A nation is judged for what it does; the family history explains why the deed was such a betrayal.

pos: n. (a Reubenite brother of Dathan and Abiram; also a son of Simeon)
etymology: Hebrew Nemuel, of uncertain meaning; the same Simeonite is called Jemuel in Genesis. The Reubenite bearer is named only to locate him beside two men whose rebellion the wilderness did not forget.
biblical_def: The census of Numbers 26 pauses over one family long enough to retell an old story: “And the sons of Eliab; Nemuel, and Dathan, and Abiram. This is that Dathan and Abiram, which were famous in the congregation, who strove against Moses and against Aaron in the company of Korah, when they strove against the LORD” (Numbers 26:9). Nemuel is the brother who is not in that sentence. The second bearer heads a Simeonite family: “The sons of Simeon after their families: of Nemuel, the family of the Nemuelites: of Jamin, the family of the Jaminites: of Jachin, the family of the Jachinites” (Numbers 26:12). The Chronicler lists him again: “The sons of Simeon were, Nemuel, and Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, and Shaul” (1 Chronicles 4:24). The census then records what happened to the rebels, and adds a clause that has kept generations of readers reading: “And the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up together with Korah, when that company died, what time the fire devoured two hundred and fifty men: and they became a sign. Notwithstanding the children of Korah died not” (Numbers 26:10-11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Nemuel; the name belongs to a Reubenite brother of Dathan and Abiram, and to a son of Simeon.
webster_full: NEMUEL, n. A son of Eliab the Reubenite, and brother of Dathan and Abiram; also a son of Simeon.
SEDITION, n. A factious commotion of the people; a tumultuous assembly of men rising in opposition to law.
CONGREGATION, n. A collection or assembly of separate things; the whole body of the people of Israel.
SIGN, n. A token; something by which another thing is shown or represented; a memorial warning.
REMONSTRANCE, n. Show; discovery; a strong representation of reasons against a measure.
scriptures: Numbers 26:9

And the sons of Eliab; Nemuel, and Dathan, and Abiram. This is that Dathan and Abiram, which were famous in the congregation, who strove against Moses and against Aaron in the company of Korah, when they strove against the LORD:
Numbers 26:12
The sons of Simeon after their families: of Nemuel, the family of the Nemuelites: of Jamin, the family of the Jaminites: of Jachin, the family of the Jachinites:
1 Chronicles 4:24
The sons of Simeon were, Nemuel, and Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, and Shaul:
Numbers 26:11
Notwithstanding the children of Korah died not.
corruption_summary: Rebellion against appointed authority is admired as courage and independence, when Numbers calls the same men famous in the congregation and records exactly what became of them.
corruption_paragraphs: The census of Numbers 26 uses a striking word for Dathan and Abiram: they were famous in the congregation. They were not fringe agitators but renowned men, princes of the assembly, men of renown, and their complaint was populist and superficially pious — all the congregation are holy, every one of them, wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the congregation of the LORD. Every element of it is recognisable. The text's judgment is equally plain: they strove against Moses and against Aaron, and in doing so they strove against the LORD.

The name itself faces no postmodern redefinition. Two things should be held together here. Scripture condemns the rebellion of Korah, Dathan and Abiram against the men God had appointed, and Jude uses it as a type of false teachers who despise dominion. Scripture also records Nemuel, their own brother, who is simply named and not swallowed, and adds four words at the end of the account that have comforted readers ever since: notwithstanding the children of Korah died not. Judgment fell where it was aimed and nowhere else, and the sons of the chief rebel later led Israel's praise.

pos: n. (a Gershonite Levite head; also an ancestor of Joshua)
etymology: Hebrew Ladan, of uncertain meaning; the same Levite appears elsewhere as Libni. He heads one of the two Gershonite houses in David's reorganisation of the temple service.
biblical_def: One bearer stands in Ephraim's line, three generations above Joshua: “Laadan his son, Ammihud his son, Elishama his son” (1 Chronicles 7:26). The better-known Laadan heads a Levitical house: “Of the Gershonites were, Laadan, and Shimei” (1 Chronicles 23:7), and his own sons are named: “The sons of Laadan; the chief was Jehiel, and Zetham, and Joel, three” (1 Chronicles 23:8). The chapter he belongs to is one of the most consequential administrative acts in the Old Testament. David, old and full of days, numbered the Levites and assigned them by courses, and the reason he gave changed what the tribe would do for the next thousand years: “For David said, The LORD God of Israel hath given rest unto his people, that they may dwell in Jerusalem for ever” (1 Chronicles 23:25). The Levites had existed to carry the tabernacle from place to place. With a permanent house coming, their work was reorganised toward song, gatekeeping, courts and instruction.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Laadan; the name belongs to a head of the Gershonite Levites and to an ancestor of Joshua.
webster_full: LAADAN, n. A head of the Gershonite Levites in David's reorganisation of the temple service.
GERSHONITES, n. The family of Levites descended from Gershon, the eldest son of Levi.
COURSE, n. Order of succession; a series of appointed turns, as of priests and Levites on duty.
REST, n. Cessation of labor or motion; quiet; repose; the rest promised to the people of God.
REORGANIZE, v.t. To organize anew; to reduce again to a regular body or system.
scriptures: 1 Chronicles 7:26
Laadan his son, Ammihud his son, Elishama his son,
1 Chronicles 23:7
Of the Gershonites were, Laadan, and Shimei.
1 Chronicles 23:8
The sons of Laadan; the chief was Jehiel, and Zetham, and Joel, three.
1 Chronicles 23:25
For David said, The LORD God of Israel hath given rest unto his people, that they may dwell in Jerusalem for ever:
corruption_summary: Change in the forms of ministry is resisted as unfaithfulness, or embraced as an end in itself, where Scripture shows a reorganisation made for a stated theological reason.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how 1 Chronicles 23 reasons about change. The Levites' original charge was portage — bearing the tabernacle, its boards, hangings and vessels, through the wilderness. David reassigns them, and he gives the ground in one sentence: the LORD God of Israel hath given rest unto His people, that they may dwell in Jerusalem for ever. The circumstance God had granted changed, so the shape of the service changed, and the change was made deliberately and on a theological premise rather than from restlessness.

Both modern errors are rebuked by that. The congregation that treats every inherited arrangement as untouchable would have kept four thousand men trained to carry boards for a tent that no longer moved. The congregation that changes for novelty's sake has no premise at all; David had one, and it was about what God had done. The Reformed rule holds the line between them: the elements of worship are fixed by Scripture and not open to invention, while the circumstances — hours, order, arrangement, division of labour — are to be ordered by the light of nature and Christian prudence. Laadan's house is what that looks like in practice.

pos: n. (a son of Naphtali and head of the Gunites; also a Gadite)
etymology: Hebrew Guni, perhaps meaning protected or coloured. He is one of the four sons of Naphtali who went down into Egypt with Jacob, and his family is counted in the wilderness census.
biblical_def: He is named among the seventy souls who went down to Egypt: “And the sons of Naphtali; Jahzeel, and Guni, and Jezer, and Shillem” (Genesis 46:24). Four hundred years later the family is counted as a clan in the wilderness: “Of the sons of Naphtali after their families: of Jahzeel, the family of the Jahzeelites: of Guni, the family of the Gunites” (Numbers 26:48). A man of the same name heads a Gadite house east of Jordan: “Ahi the son of Abdiel, the son of Guni, chief of the house of their fathers” (1 Chronicles 5:15). The distance between the first two verses is the point. A single man walked into Egypt in a family of seventy, and his descendants came out as one of the numbered clans of a nation, exactly as God had said they would: “And God spake unto Israel in the visions of the night, and said, Jacob, Jacob. And he said, Here am I. And he said, I am God, the God of thy father: fear not to go down into Egypt; for I will there make of thee a great nation” (Genesis 46:2-3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Guni; the name belongs to a son of Naphtali and to a Gadite chief.
webster_full: GUNI, n. A son of Naphtali, head of the family of the Gunites.
NAPHTALI, n. The sixth son of Jacob, and the tribe descended from him, settled in the north of Canaan.
CLAN, n. A race; a family; a tribe; a body of persons united by a common ancestor.
CENSUS, n. An enumeration of the inhabitants of a country; a numbering of the people by families.
MULTIPLY, v.i. To increase in number; to extend; to grow or become more numerous.
scriptures: Genesis 46:24
And the sons of Naphtali; Jahzeel, and Guni, and Jezer, and Shillem.
Numbers 26:48
Of the sons of Naphtali after their families: of Jahzeel, the family of the Jahzeelites: of Guni, the family of the Gunites:
1 Chronicles 5:15
Ahi the son of Abdiel, the son of Guni, chief of the house of their fathers.
Genesis 46:3
And he said, I am God, the God of thy father: fear not to go down into Egypt; for I will there make of thee a great nation:
corruption_summary: The promise of increase in Egypt is read as national myth, when Scripture presents it as a word spoken to a frightened old man in a night vision and afterwards audited by census.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the genealogies function as an audit of a promise. God told Jacob at Beersheba, on the way down to Egypt, not to fear, because He would there make of him a great nation. Genesis 46 then lists the seventy souls who went — Guni among four sons of Naphtali — and Numbers 26 lists the same names again as clans, with numbers attached, at the far end of the wilderness. The promise is stated, the starting figure is recorded, and the result is counted.

This is the habitual method of the Old Testament and one reason its lists deserve more patience than they get. God speaks; time passes, often centuries; the text records the outcome and expects the reader to make the connection. Guni is a name and nothing more — no story, no words, no recorded act. What his name does is prove that the God who spoke in the visions of the night to a man afraid of a journey kept exactly what He said, and that the keeping could be counted family by family four hundred years later.

pos: n. (a Horite chief of Seir; also a son of Jerahmeel in Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Onam, meaning vigorous or strong. Two unrelated men bear it — one in the Horite genealogy of Edom, one in the line of Judah through Jerahmeel.
biblical_def: The first belongs to the aboriginal inhabitants of Mount Seir, whom Esau's descendants displaced: “And the children of Shobal were these; Alvan, and Manahath, and Ebal, Shepho, and Onam” (Genesis 36:23). The Chronicler repeats the list with slight variation in spelling: “The sons of Shobal; Alian, and Manahath, and Ebal, Shephi, and Onam. And the sons of Zibeon; Aiah, and Anah” (1 Chronicles 1:40). The second is in Judah's line: “Jerahmeel had also another wife, whose name was Atarah; she was the mother of Onam” (1 Chronicles 2:26). That Scripture preserves the Horite genealogy at all is worth noticing; these were not Israelites, not covenant people, and not even the Edomites who supplanted them. Moses records their chiefs by name, as he records the sons of Japheth and the sons of Ham, because the whole earth is of one blood: “And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Acts 17:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Onam; the Hebrew signifies vigorous, and the name belongs to a Horite chief and to a man of Judah.
webster_full: ONAM, n. A Horite chief of Mount Seir; also a son of Jerahmeel in the tribe of Judah.
HORITES, n. The original inhabitants of Mount Seir, dispossessed by the descendants of Esau.
ABORIGINAL, a. First; original; primitive; applied to the earliest known inhabitants of a country.
GENEALOGY, n. An account or history of the descent of a person or family from an ancestor.
NATION, n. A body of people inhabiting the same country, united under one government.
scriptures: Genesis 36:23
And the children of Shobal were these; Alvan, and Manahath, and Ebal, Shepho, and Onam.
1 Chronicles 1:40
The sons of Shobal; Alian, and Manahath, and Ebal, Shephi, and Onam. And the sons of Zibeon; Aiah, and Anah.
1 Chronicles 2:26
Jerahmeel had also another wife, whose name was Atarah; she was the mother of Onam.
Acts 17:26
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
corruption_summary: Race is treated as a fundamental category of human identity, against a canon that traces every nation to one man and one blood and keeps the genealogies of peoples outside the covenant.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary rejects the frameworks — whether the older racialism or its current inversion — that make race an irreducible category determining guilt, standing or identity. Scripture's anthropology is one-in-Adam and one-in-Christ. Paul told the Athenians that God made of one blood all nations of men to dwell on the face of the earth and determined the bounds of their habitation, which makes every national difference a matter of providence rather than of essence, and every human being a descendant of the same first parents.

The name itself faces no postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity Scripture quietly extends to outsiders by recording them. Onam the Horite was not a covenant man; his people were dispossessed by Esau's and left no scripture, no prophets and no promises. Moses names his father and his brothers anyway, as he names the seventy nations of Genesis 10. The Bible's interest in who people were and where they came from is not confined to the elect line, because the God who chose Abraham also appointed the times and bounds of the Horites of Seir.

pos: n. (a son of Ishmael; also a Simeonite)
etymology: Hebrew Mibsam, meaning sweet odour or balsam. He is fourth in the list of Ishmael's twelve sons, each of whom became a prince of a tribe.
biblical_def: He is named in the register of Ishmael's house: “And these are the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their names, according to their generations: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebajoth; and Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam” (Genesis 25:13). The Chronicler repeats the list: “These are their generations: The firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth; then Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam” (1 Chronicles 1:29). A Simeonite of the same name appears in Judah's south country: “Shallum his son, Mibsam his son, Mishma his son” (1 Chronicles 4:25). The twelve sons of Ishmael are counted and summarised exactly as the twelve sons of Jacob are, and the reason is a promise God made to Abraham about the son who was not the son of promise: “And as for Ishmael, I have heard thee: Behold, I have blessed him, and will make him fruitful, and will multiply him exceedingly; twelve princes shall he beget, and I will make him a great nation” (Genesis 17:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Mibsam; the Hebrew signifies sweet odour, and the name belongs to a son of Ishmael and to a Simeonite.
webster_full: MIBSAM, n. A son of Ishmael, and prince of a tribe; in Hebrew, sweet odour or balsam.
ISHMAEL, n. The son of Abraham by Hagar, and the father of twelve princes of the Arabian tribes.
PRINCE, n. The chief of a body of men; the ruler of a tribe or people.
PROMISE, n. A declaration which gives to the person to whom it is made a right to expect the performance of some act.
COMMON GRACE, the favor of God shown to all men in providence, distinguished from saving grace.
scriptures: Genesis 25:13
And these are the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their names, according to their generations: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebajoth; and Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam,
1 Chronicles 1:29
These are their generations: The firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth; then Kedar, and Adbeel, and Mibsam,
1 Chronicles 4:25
Shallum his son, Mibsam his son, Mishma his son.
Genesis 17:20
And as for Ishmael, I have heard thee: Behold, I have blessed him, and will make him fruitful, and will multiply him exceedingly ; twelve princes shall he beget, and I will make him a great nation.
corruption_summary: Election is caricatured as God's indifference to everyone outside the chosen line, when He blessed Ishmael by name, heard Hagar in the wilderness, and kept the count of twelve princes.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest objection to unconditional election is that it makes God callous toward the non-elect, and the Ishmael narratives are the best answer Scripture gives. God says plainly that His covenant will be established with Isaac, and in the same breath says of the other son: as for Ishmael, I have heard thee, behold I have blessed him. He heard the boy crying in the wilderness of Beersheba, opened Hagar's eyes to a well, was with the lad as he grew, and produced from him twelve princes and a great nation — and then had Moses write their names down, Mibsam among them.

The name itself faces no postmodern redefinition. The distinction the dictionary keeps is the historic one between common grace and saving grace. God gives rain to the just and the unjust, makes His sun to rise on the evil and the good, grants nations their appointed times and bounds, and is good to men who will never confess Him. None of that is the covenant, and none of it saves. But it is real kindness from a real God, and any presentation of election that cannot say so has not read Genesis 17 and 21 carefully. The son who was not chosen was blessed, named, numbered, and buried by his brother beside their father.

pos: n. (a Levite under Hezekiah; also a priestly house after the exile)
etymology: Hebrew Minyamin, a shortened form of Benjamin, son of the right hand. The name belongs to a Levite trusted with distribution under Hezekiah and to a priestly course after the return.
biblical_def: Hezekiah's reformation produced such a quantity of tithes and offerings that a distribution system had to be built, and this man was one of those trusted with it: “And next him were Eden, and Miniamin, and Jeshua, and Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah, in the cities of the priests, in their set office, to give to their brethren by courses, as well to the great as to the small” (2 Chronicles 31:15). The clause as well to the great as to the small is the standard the whole arrangement was held to. A priestly house of the name returns in Nehemiah's register: “Of Abijah, Zichri; of Miniamin, of Moadiah, Piltai” (Nehemiah 12:17). And at the dedication of the wall a priest of the name blows a trumpet in the great procession: “And the priests; Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Michaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah, with trumpets” (Nehemiah 12:41). The reason there was anything to distribute in Hezekiah's day is given a few verses earlier: “And as soon as the commandment came abroad, the children of Israel brought in abundance the firstfruits of corn, wine, and oil, and honey, and of all the increase of the field; and the tithe of all things brought they in abundantly” (2 Chronicles 31:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Miniamin; the name is a form of Benjamin, and belongs to a Levite under Hezekiah and to a priestly house.
webster_full: MINIAMIN, n. A Levite in the reign of Hezekiah, set over the distribution of the offerings.
TITHE, n. The tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock, allotted to the clergy.
FIRSTFRUITS, n. The fruit or produce first matured and collected in any season, offered to God.
DISTRIBUTION, n. The act of dividing among a number; dispensation; the dealing out to several persons.
IMPARTIAL, a. Not partial; not biased in favor of one party more than another; equitable; just.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 31:15

And next him were Eden, and Miniamin, and Jeshua, and Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah, in the cities of the priests, in their set office, to give to their brethren by courses, as well to the great as to the small:
Nehemiah 12:17
Of Abijah, Zichri; of Miniamin, of Moadiah, Piltai;
Nehemiah 12:41
And the priests; Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Michaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah, with trumpets;
2 Chronicles 31:5

And as soon as the commandment came abroad, the children of Israel brought in abundance the firstfruits of corn, wine, and oil, and honey, and of all the increase of the field; and the tithe of all things brought they in abundantly.
corruption_summary: Giving is treated as a private transaction with no accounting attached, when Scripture names the men who handled the offerings and records the rule they distributed by.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the care Scripture takes over money given to God. Hezekiah did not simply receive the offerings; he appointed chambers, prepared them, set Conaniah over them with his brother Shimei as second, and named ten men including Miniamin who were in their set office to give to their brethren by courses. Paul does the same thing with the collection for Jerusalem, travelling with appointed men and stating his reason: providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men.

The standard the Chronicler records is worth more than the administrative detail: as well to the great as to the small. Distribution was by course and by need, and rank did not alter the portion. James says a congregation that seats a man with a gold ring better than a poor man in vile raiment has become a judge with evil thoughts. Where offerings are handled without accounting, or distributed with respect of persons, the church has departed from a pattern the Old Testament laid down in careful prose and named the responsible men in.
